root_cause.text: `memfd_luo_preserve_folios()` in the `mm/memfd_luo` subsystem serialized each folio’s dirty state from the folio/PTE state at preserve time instead of treating preserved memfd folios as always dirty, so a folio that was clean when preserved but dirtied later could be restored as reclaimable clean memory and lose user data under page reclaim.
root_cause.evidence: The patch comment explicitly says “memfd preservation with LUO saves the flag at preserve(). This is problematic. The folio might get dirtied later,” and explains that “After retrieve, the next kernel will see the folio as clean and might try to reclaim it under memory pressure. This will result in losing user data.” The diff fixes this by removing the conditional `if (folio_test_dirty(folio)) flags |= MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY;` and unconditionally calling `folio_mark_dirty(folio);` and setting `pfolio->flags = MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY | MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_UPTODATE;`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Remove an unused local variable from `memfd_luo_preserve_folios()`.
intent_record.what: The local variable `unsigned int flags = 0;` was removed from the `memfd_luo_preserve_folios()` loop body. No other code in the shown hunk was changed.
intent_record.how: This change has no runtime behavior impact in the shown code, because the removed variable was not used anywhere in the loop. It eliminates an unused declaration and may avoid a compiler warning.

intent_record.intent_summary: Unconditionally mark preserved folios dirty to prevent post-retrieve reclaim from losing user data during live update.
intent_record.what: Inside memfd_luo_preserve_folios(), the conditional check `if (folio_test_dirty(folio)) flags |= MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY;` was removed and replaced with a comment explaining the rationale plus an unconditional call to `folio_mark_dirty(folio);` while the folio is locked.
intent_record.how: At runtime, every preserved folio is now marked dirty regardless of its prior state, so the saved metadata will treat it as user-owned data after live update. This prevents a folio that was clean at preserve time but dirtied later from being mistakenly reclaimable after retrieve, avoiding potential loss of user data, though it makes clean folios non-reclaimable afterward.

intent_record.intent_summary: Always mark preserved folios as dirty and uptodate when recording them in memfd_luo_preserve_folios().
intent_record.what: In memfd_luo_preserve_folios(), the code no longer ORs MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_UPTODATE into the local flags variable, and instead assigns pfolio->flags unconditionally to MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY | MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_UPTODATE.
intent_record.how: At runtime, every preserved folio is now recorded as both dirty and uptodate regardless of the prior flag state carried in the local variable. This removes dependence on the accumulated flags value and ensures the stored pfolio metadata always marks the folio as writable/modified and valid.

relevance_review.reason: The change only removes an unused स्थानीय variable and does not affect how preserved memfd folios are marked dirty or restored, so it does not address the data-loss root cause.

The change directly matches the root cause: it fixes memfd_luo_preserve_folios() by treating preserved folios as always dirty (and uptodate) instead of serializing their dirty state at preserve time, preventing later reclaim from losing user data.

candidates.rationale: This conditional makes the preserved folio's dirty flag depend on its state at preserve time. Under the reported bug, a folio clean at preservation but dirtied afterward could later be restored without being treated as dirty, enabling reclaim to drop user data.

Although the root cause is about dirty-state serialization, this pre-fix conditional-style handling of folio state during preservation shows the same pattern of recording transient state instead of conservatively preserving it; it could allow a preserved folio to be restored as if safely reclaimable.

vuln_statements.explanation: This conditional makes preservation of the dirty bit depend on the folio's dirty state at preserve time. That matches the root cause: a folio that is clean when preserved but dirtied later can be restored without being treated as dirty, allowing reclaim to drop user data.

This statement records folio state during preservation in a way that can reflect transient conditions rather than conservatively treating preserved folios as dirty. In the vulnerable flow, that contributes to restoring preserved memory as reclaimable clean memory and losing data under reclaim.

bic_trace_step.reason: The vulnerable construct is present in the shown code. In `memfd_luo_preserve_folios()`, the code serializes dirty state from the folio at preserve time: `if (folio_test_dirty(folio)) flags |= MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY;` and later stores it into `pfolio->flags = flags;`. Then on restore, `memfd_luo_retrieve_folios()` only re-marks the folio dirty if that saved flag was set: `if (flags & MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY) folio_mark_dirty(folio);`. This means a folio that was clean when preserved but dirtied later can be restored without the dirty bit, matching the root cause. There is no indication here that preserved memfd folios are treated as always dirty, so the fix is not present in this commit.

bic_trace_step.reason: The shown function already contains the fix for the reported memfd_luo folio-state preservation issue. The vulnerable construct was saving folio state based on the folio/PTE at preserve time and allowing a later-clean folio to be restored without the correct state. In this snippet, the code now unconditionally makes every preserved folio uptodate: it takes the folio lock (`folio_lock(folio);`), checks `if (!folio_test_uptodate(folio))`, then zeroes the folio, flushes cache, and marks it uptodate (`folio_mark_uptodate(folio);`), followed by `flags |= MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_UPTODATE;`. This removes the possibility of preserving a non-uptodate folio state that could later be restored as clean/zeroed memory and lose data. The dirty-flag logic shown (`if (folio_test_dirty(folio)) flags |= MEMFD_LUO_FOLIO_DIRTY;`) is not the vulnerable condition described in the root cause, and the relevant uptodate handling is already corrected here.
